extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students studying equity procedure in patent infringement suits
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing practice, evidence, decrees, rehearings, and remedies in equity suits for patent infringement; guidance on admissibility of evidence, types/effects of decrees, and standards for reopening or rehearing cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to examiner for additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the motion of either party, for sufficient cause, the court may refer the record back to the examiner for the introduction of additional evidence or the re-examination of the former witnesses, and in such reference the testimony must be limited to the points designated by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is appropriate when evidence is equally accessible to both parties and connection with controversy is apparent; referral limited in scope by court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect notice must be amended or evidence excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: If a witness is objected to before the examiner on the ground that the notice is imperfect, the notice must be amended or the evidence though taken will not be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example case cited: Eiesele v. Haas (1887). An imperfect notice objection before examination requires amendment to preserve the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to suppress testimony for witness mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to suppress testimony on the ground that the witness was mistaken as to the occasion named is not allowed if the examination was in proper form and after due notice and on oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examination complied with formalities (proper form, due notice, oath), mere mistake as to occasion doesn't justify suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use evidence taken without due notice is inadmissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of prior use taken in against objection before the examiner, without due notice or answer, will be struck out by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court strikes out evidence of prior use when party lacked due notice or a proper answer; see Bragg v. City of Stockton (1886).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent not offered to examiner and not in answer cannot be introduced in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent not offered as evidence before the examiner, and not set up in the answer, cannot be introduced in equity, even upon a question of title, as the plaintiff has no opportunity for explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the opposing party had no chance to address the patent because it wasn't in the record or pleadings, it should be excluded; see Grover & Baker Sewing Machine Co. v. Sloat (1860).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original patent may be offered at hearing to show re-issue departure when no surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may offer the original at the hearing to show that the re-issue departs from it, though it was not put in before the master, if it works no surprise to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering originals late can be allowed if it does not unfairly surprise the opposing party; see Enapp v. Shaw (1883).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence by persons not named in the answer may be considered unless struck
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of prior use, etc., given by persons not named in the answer, will be considered on the hearing unless a motion is made to strike it out, although it was objected to when taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of witnesses not listed in answer does not automatically bar their testimony; adversary must move to strike to exclude it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improperly noticed evidence not validated by later amendment except when designated by court
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of prior use taken without proper notice and objected to cannot be admitted under the answer when afterward amended on motion, unless designated by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amending the answer after the fact does not retroactively legitimize improperly noticed evidence unless the court permits designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing papers after hearing/submission requires leave of court
rubrics_metrics.description: After the hearing and submission neither party has the right to file any paper in the case without leave of the court, upon motion and due notice to the adversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibition on filings commences at submission date and continues while cause remains on the docket; exceptions require court leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity practice generally follows English chancery pre-New Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice in equity, in actions for infringement, follows that of the English chancery as it existed before the 'New Rules', except where changed by express regulations; rules prescribed by the Supreme Court are binding on the Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges conferred by these rules and objections for their violation must be made available before or at the hearing, or they will be waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written stipulations recognized; parol stipulations not enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: Stipulations of the parties, when properly evidenced (written and filed), are recognized by the court, but parol stipulations made out of court, and concerning disputed terms, will not be enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parol stipulations lacking record evidence are not noticed by the court as binding; written on-record stipulations can have binding effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of decrees in equity for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Decrees in equity in actions for infringement are of three kinds: Decrees pro confesso; Interlocutory Decrees; and Final Decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type has distinct grounds, effects, and procedural consequences described separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for decree pro confesso
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree pro confesso may be granted where the defendant, having been served with process, fails to appear within the time required, or having appeared fails to plead, demur, or answer according to the order of the court, or fails to answer after a former demurrer, plea, or answer has been overruled or declared insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a decree assumes the truth of the bill and continues binding unless set aside by a bill of review or for fraud; discretion exists for allowing an answer later but denial is not appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and conclusiveness of decree pro confesso
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree pro confesso assumes the truth of the bill and concludes the defendant as to matters supported by the allegations of the bill, taking them to be true; it cannot be collaterally impeached and is binding until rescinded on proper grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is as binding as any solemn decree and can only be attacked by bill of review or petition to rescind for fraud; while in force defendant cannot deny validity of patent or diligence in obtaining it except as appears on the face of the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for interlocutory decree
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decree is a decree in favor of the plaintiff upon the issues created by the bill and answer, and referring the cause to a master for an account of profits and award of damages; plaintiff is entitled to it if the evidence sustains the patentability of the invention, validity of the patent, title of the plaintiff, alleged infringement, and necessity for equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any infringement, however slight, entitles plaintiff to a decree; where multiple patents/claims are alleged, decree on any valid infringed claim must be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory decree and multiple claims/patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the bill counts on several patents or on several claims of the same patent, and either patent or any claim is found to be valid and to have been violated, a decree must be granted and an account ordered upon such claim or patent, although the others are invalid or have not been infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive claims do not impair right to decree on proper claims if disclaimer filed without unreasonable delay; presence of multiple patents can complicate injunction relief if one patent is near expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of interlocutory decree
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decree can cover only the patent and the patented articles in suit; it does not cover any other patented articles or patents except those in suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant justifies under a license, the court may order account of overdue license fees instead of profits; a decree under general relief can order accounting for all profits from violation described in bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with excessive claims and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of excessive claims does not impair the right to a decree upon a proper claim of the same patent, on filing a disclaimer of the excess, unless such disclaimer has already been unreasonably delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay or omission to disclaim is a question of fact and must be raised by the answer; invalid claims must be disclaimed before decree will be granted when delay is unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final decree and requirement of account
rubrics_metrics.description: A final decree is one which terminates the litigation by awarding profits, damages, and other permanent relief; a final decree for plaintiff cannot be granted where an account is necessary until the account has been taken by the master and reported to and accepted by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final decrees for defendants can be entered at conclusion of hearing when any one of defendant's defenses is sustained; the court will dismiss the bill rather than decide claims solely to establish precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decree for defendant and effect on remaining claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant has a right to a final decree if he sustains any one of his defenses (e.g., against patentability, validity, title, alleged infringement, or equitable right), and the court will dismiss the bill and leave plaintiff to other remedies rather than pass on plaintiff claims to create precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will not pass on claims it thinks evidence sustains if it results in dismissal; where patent plainly void on face, bill dismissed regardless of answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearings before final decree
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing may be ordered at any time between the interlocutory and the final decree for the purpose of admitting new evidence or additional defenses, or on any other sufficient grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearing after final decree must be granted at same term at which decree rendered if case appealable to Supreme Court, otherwise may be permitted next term; allowance of rehearing is discretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may move for a rehearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person interested in the action and conducting it at his expense, though not a party to the record, may move for a rehearing, and if he does not, will be bound by the decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A funder or interested party who provided money to carry on the suit may apply for rehearing; failure to move binds them to the decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for rehearing based on newly discovered evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: No rehearing on this ground will be granted where the alleged new evidence is immaterial or cumulative, or would not lead to a change in the decree, or was known to the party or his counsel at the former hearing, or could then have been discovered and presented by the exercise of proper diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use evidence that is less persuasive than former trial generally won't support rehearing; cumulative or immaterial evidence and evidence discoverable earlier by diligence are barred; courts require new evidence would change result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and diligence for rehearing motions
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for a rehearing will not be granted unless presented within the time fixed by law, and due diligence is required in presenting grounds for rehearing; four years' delay has been held too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity Rule 88 requires application for rehearing at same term as final decree when appeal possible; undue delay undermines requests to reopen decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearings limited to matters that would change decree
rubrics_metrics.description: No rehearing will be allowed unless the matters presented would change the decree; rehearing is discretionary and will be denied if new matters would not alter outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If newly presented matters are merely technical or would not affect the decree, courts refuse to reopen; rehearing after injunction/account decree also discretionary and limited to matters that would change decree.
